description: As aspiring innovators, we aim to transform NASA's open data into meaningful insights and innovative solutions. We enjoy brainstorming ideas, learning new technologies, and collaborating to build projects that make a difference.
summary:
AstroVanta — Monsoon Lens
AstroVanta is an interactive project for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026’s “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. It explores how June–September rainfall changed from 1981 to 2025 across a sample area in central and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
The app uses daily NASA POWER precipitation data to show:
- A rainfall trend map of 49 model grid cells and five city references: Ayodhya, Lucknow, Prayagraj, Gorakhpur, and Varanasi.
- Annual rainfall by year, plus a comparison of the 1981–1990 and 2016–2025 averages.
- Trend estimates, 95% uncertainty intervals, charts, and CSV downloads.
Trends use the Theil–Sen method with a circular five-year moving-block bootstrap for uncertainty. Results are descriptive: the grid is a rectangular sample, NASA POWER values are model estimates rather than local rain-gauge measurements, and the analysis does not explain why rainfall changed.
details:
AstroVanta — Monsoon Lens

AstroVanta is an interactive browser app that explores how monsoon rainfall has changed across a sample of the Indo-Gangetic Plain around Ayodhya. It uses daily precipitation data from NASA POWER for complete June–September seasons from 1981 to 2025. The app totals each season’s rainfall, maps trends across 49 regional grid cells, and includes five city reference locations: Ayodhya, Lucknow, Prayagraj, Gorakhpur, and Varanasi. Users can inspect annual rainfall charts, explore rainfall by year, compare 1981–1990 with 2016–2025, and download results as CSV.

To estimate long-term trends, AstroVanta uses the Theil–Sen slope and an exploratory 95% interval calculated with a circular five-year moving-block bootstrap. It labels a trend as increasing or decreasing only when the interval excludes zero; otherwise, it is marked unclear.

The project makes decades of climate data easier to explore and helps people see that rainfall can change differently from place to place. It is designed to support climate learning and informed questions about regional change. Its results are descriptive: they do not explain why rainfall changed or predict future rainfall.

We built the app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It requests precipitation data from the NASA POWER API; Leaflet and OpenStreetMap provide the interactive map. We used a web browser and a local Python HTTP server during development. The project requires no special hardware.

Our creative idea is captured by the phrase “One monsoon. Many trajectories.” The app brings a regional map, individual location charts, year-by-year views, period comparisons, and uncertainty into one experience, making both differences and limitations visible.

We considered the limits of model-based rainfall estimates, the fact that our rectangular study area does not cover the entire Indo-Gangetic Plain, and the uncertainty in estimating trends from a finite record. We also account for the API’s one-year request limit and note that grid-cell intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
